proof:
# Supporting facets retain a volume contribution after Minkowski addition

This note records a necessary geometric budget for actual three-fiber
critical caps. It does not prove OC. The supporting facet has zero
d-volume but must not be replaced by an empty set.

## 1. An exact sectional formula and its all-dimensional consequence

Let d>=2. Let D be a full-dimensional compact convex body in R^d, and
let F be a compact convex body in an affine hyperplane perpendicular
to a unit vector e. Write f=H_(d-1)(F)>0 and

    h=max_D e.x-min_D e.x>0,  U=|D|.

Translate F so its e-coordinate is zero. For a real t, the section of
D+F at e-coordinate t is EXACTLY D_t+F, where D_t is identified with
the perpendicular (d-1)-space. The reason is that every point of F
has zero e-coordinate; no union over different heights occurs.
Fubini and Brunn--Minkowski in dimension m=d-1 therefore give

    |D+F| >= integral (|D_t|^(1/m)+f^(1/m))^m dt
            >= U+fh.                                      (1)

The integral is over the open height interval of D. Every section
there is full-dimensional in the perpendicular space: interpolate
an interior ball with points on either side of the chosen height.
The two endpoint heights have one-dimensional measure zero. All sets
are compact and all functions are measurable, so Fubini applies.

More precisely the first lower bound in (1) equals

    U+fh+sum_(j=1)^(m-1) binom(m,j) f^(j/m)
                              integral |D_t|^((m-j)/m) dt. (2)

These additional terms are nonnegative. For d=2, m=1 and the sum
is empty; addition of two intervals adds their lengths. Thus

    |D+F|=U+fh                      when d=2.             (3)

No nonempty zero-volume section has been discarded in deriving the
formula. The d=1 case is excluded because its supporting face is a
point and (1) with two separate endpoint terms would be incorrect.

## 2. Apply the formula to one actual mixed cap

Let A,K,B be full-dimensional compact convex bodies in R^d with
(A+B)/2 subset K. Fix u!=0 and levels a0,b0, and put c0=(a0+b0)/2.
Suppose

    D=A intersect {u.x>=a0} is a proper positive-volume cap,
    B subset {u.x<=b0},
    F=B intersect {u.x=b0} has positive H_(d-1)-measure f.

Then

    (D+F)/2 subset K intersect {u.x>=c0}.

Indeed the midpoint inclusion gives membership in K, and averaging
the two scalar inequalities gives the cap inequality. The normal
height of D is h=(h_A(u)-a0)/||u||: properness ensures that its
minimum is a0 and its maximum is the support height of A.
Consequently, writing U=|D| and q=|K intersect {u.x>=c0}|,

    q >= 2^(-d)(U+ f(h_A(u)-a0)/||u||).                  (4)

The sharper bound (2) is available in the same formula. For d=2,
the right side in (4) is exactly the area of the contained Minkowski
set. It need not equal q, since K can be larger.

Place A,K,B at integer bases -1,0,1. A through-middle halfspace with
these three thresholds captures U,q,0 respectively. If it attains
raw depth Q, then Q=U+q and (4) gives

    2^d Q >= (2^d+1)U+ f(h_A(u)-a0)/||u||.             (5)

This conclusion is valid for the original closed ambient halfspace;
the zero B-volume is a supporting facet, not an empty restriction.
No symmetry, centroid condition, or local differentiability is needed
for (4)-(5). Criticality enters only to identify its mass with Q.

## 3. Planar simplex normalization

Let

    T={x<=1, y<=1, -x-y<=1},
    v1=(1,0), v2=(0,1), v3=(-1,-1),  b=|T|=9/2.

Suppose B=T, and consider the three ambient caps v_i.x>=z.
Their restrictions have thresholds -1,0,1 on A,K,B. Put

    a=|A|, k=|K|,
    U_i=|A intersect {v_i.x>=-1}|,
    q_i=|K intersect {v_i.x>=0}|,
    h_i=h_A(v_i), S=h1+h2+h3.

When the A restrictions are proper, the B restrictions are its full
facets. Every facet has length divided by ||v_i|| equal to3. Hence

    q_i >= [U_i+3(h_i+1)]/4.

If all three caps have the same actual critical mass Q, this is

    4Q >=5U_i+3(h_i+1)             for i=1,2,3.          (6)

For a smaller B contained in T, replace3 by the actual supporting
facet length divided by ||v_i||; the fixed value3 cannot be retained.

## 4. Exact mixed area of A and T

For every planar compact convex body A,

    |(A+T)/2|=(a+b+3S)/4.                              (7)

Here is a short justification of the mixed-area formula being used.
For two polygons the cyclic edge list of a positive Minkowski sum is
the merge of the two cyclic edge lists, combining parallel edges.
On this fixed cyclic list every vertex is affine in the positive
scaling parameter. The shoelace area is thus a polynomial of degree
at most two. The constant and quadratic coefficients of |T+tA| are
b and a, the latter also following after division by t^2 and passage
to infinity. The linear coefficient is the first area variation of T:
each facet sweeps a strip of width t h_A(n), while the neighborhoods
of its finitely many vertices contribute O(t^2). Thus that coefficient
is sum_F H_1(F)h_A(n_F)=3S. One may first translate A to contain0;
the sum is invariant under this translation because the length-weighted
outward normals of T sum to zero. Approximate arbitrary A by inscribed
polygons. Their support functions and Minkowski sums converge uniformly
and in Hausdorff distance, and planar area of bounded convex sets is
continuous. This proves the same identity for A. Set t=1 and divide
by4 to obtain (7).

In particular actual midpoint compatibility implies

    k >= (a+b+3S)/4.                                   (8)

For each positive residual R_i=A intersect {v_i.x<=-1}, write
r_i=|R_i| and S_i=sum_j h_(R_i)(v_j). Its midpoint with T lies in
the complementary middle cap, giving the further exact lower bound

    k-q_i >= (r_i+b+3S_i)/4.                           (9)

These identities use the SAME body A, not independently prescribed
one-dimensional support data. Proper A cuts ensure positive residuals.

## 5. Combine with the already proved ordinary three-cap profile

Order the U_i increasingly as U_(1)<=U_(2)<=U_(3), and set

    F=U_(1)+U_(2)+U_(3)/4.

The three middle halfplanes cover the plane because sum_i v_i=0.
The proved ordinary planar three-cap profile is

    largest(q)+middle(q)+smallest(q)/4 >= k.

Its proof and endpoint treatment are in the ordinary-profile archive
and in `candidate 4dfc7dda63b85569`.
Since q_i=Q-U_i, it yields exactly

    k <= (9/4)Q-F.                                     (10)

If Q<Gamma_2(a+b+k)/2=(2/9)(a+b+k), (10) implies

    k<a+b-2F.                                         (11)

If moreover no fiber is heavy, then k>|a-b|. Equations (8) and
(11) give the NECESSARY strict inequalities

    F<min(a,b),
    S+(8/3)F<a+b,
    max_i U_i < (4/9)(a+b-F).                          (12)

Both bounds on F follow by combining (11) with k>|a-b|. The last
inequality follows from U_i<=Q and from substituting (11) in the
strict proposed-depth upper bound. Equations (6) and (9) provide
additional necessary inequalities. The section-capacity condition
from actual integer-tilt minimality separately gives A cutting-chord
coordinate lengths at most3.

No assertion is made here that (12) is impossible for every A satisfying
those section capacities. Computational screens only test this proposed
new geometric closure; they are not a proof of it. Even a proof in this
normalized B=T branch would not resolve the arbitrary-fiber or arbitrary-
dimension OC statement.

Subsequent exact closure: the new note
`candidate 09a839b3d8f8d40a`
proves that the actual full-T, all-proper, common-cap-mass configuration
has Q>2M/9 whenever B is nonheavy. It uses a direct positive intersection
of two A residuals and (6), rather than a scalar support-data closure.
The full proof and two independent audits are complete. Its premise
B=T and the proper status of all three A cuts remain essential to the
proved statement; this does not extend the conclusion to all OC cases.
